proposals.relationship: Carter uses Cott’s history of marriage and nation to investigate how monogamous marriage was made into a contested foundation of Canadian national life.
proposals.evidence_note: Own 2008: 3–4 explicitly develops Cott’s Public Vows comparison and then states the Canadian extension; 67 uses the point that founding political orders establish marriage rules. Cott’s U.S. case is a resource, not identical Canadian evidence. The 2000 Harvard title and references are checked in Carter’s notes and bibliography; Cott’s original is not newly read. No formal mentorship or claim that every marriage followed this model.
primary_locators: Carter 2008: 3–4,67; chapter 1 notes 2–3; chapter 3 notes 4–5,14; bibliography 351

proposals.relationship: Carter adopts Perry’s Christian-conjugality formulation and uses her account of patriarchy and racial exclusion within the liberal order.
proposals.evidence_note: Own 2008: 4/note 7 identifies Perry’s specific formulation from her 2005 authored chapter in the Pickles/Rutherdale edited Contact Zones, page 115. Imperial Plots 8/notes 22–23 quotes Perry’s 2009 authored chapter in the Constant/Ducharme edited Liberalism and Hegemony, 275–276. This positive conceptual use coexists with Carter’s earlier appreciative criticism of Perry, edge_1613. No sole authorship of the edited volumes, full original chapter reading, or agreement with all Perry interpretations.
primary_locators: Carter 2016, corrected 2018: 8/notes22–23 at383; bibliography Perry entry

proposals.relationship: Carter uses Van Kirk’s analysis of changing interracial marriage to explain hostility toward Indigenous women’s marriages within the later settler order.
proposals.evidence_note: Own 2008: 6 explicitly attributes the changing hostility to Van Kirk. Chapter 1 note 12 identifies the 2006 reprint of From Marrying-In to Marrying-Out in the Gleason/Perry edited Rethinking Canada, with Van Kirk’s 1980 Many Tender Ties and Perry’s 2001 book as further resources. This is a specified historical resource within Carter’s argument, not direct mentoring, sole credit for every fur-trade marriage claim, or independent verification of those originals. Existing group comparisons are not a Van Kirk→Carter personal claim.

proposals.relationship: Carter uses Stoler’s account of colonial bourgeois formation to explain the policing of European marital dissent as well as colonized domestic life.
proposals.evidence_note: Own 2008:31/note44 and64/note1 explicitly quote Stoler and apply the argument to interracial unions and other alternatives to monogamy. The cited authored chapter is Cultivating Bourgeois Bodies and Racial Selves in Catherine Hall’s edited Cultures of Empire (2000),87–88 and90. Hall’s editorial role is distinct; the original Stoler chapter is unread here. This bounded resource does not certify all Carter’s historical generalizations or convert her whole career into a single paradigm.

proposals.relationship: Carter uses Burton’s account of unfinished colonial regulation to qualify the state’s power over Indigenous marriage and domestic life.
proposals.evidence_note: Own 2008:277 quotes and names Burton while concluding that colonial intervention disrupted without completely transforming Indigenous domestic law. Chapter7 note150 at342 cites Gender, Sexuality and Colonial Modernities (1999),1. The publisher contents identify Burton as editor and author of the introduction; this is not sole authorship of the collection. The underlying introduction and other chapters remain unread. The argument retains persistence and contestation alongside coercion, not a denial of colonial harm.

proposals.relationship: Carter uses Brown’s warning about the custom-of-the-country label to distinguish diverse understandings and durations of fur-trade unions.
proposals.evidence_note: Own 2008:31 explicitly names Brown and uses her warning about implied uniformity before differentiating lifelong, lengthy but temporary and differently understood unions. Chapter2 note47 at301 identifies Jennifer S. H. Brown’s Partial Truths: A Closer Look at Fur Trade Marriage (2002),61, distinct from her 1980 book listed with Van Kirk in note46. The original essay is unread; Carter also notes the scarcity of evidence about Indigenous wives’ perceptions. No assumption that a single marital custom governed all communities.

proposals.relationship: Carter draws on Thompson’s interpretation of English wife-sale rituals to challenge the apparent timelessness of rigid marriage and divorce rules.
proposals.evidence_note: Own 2008:65–67 explains and applies Thompson’s Customs in Common, cited in the 1993 New Press edition,404–466, with specific quotations at404,406,443 and462. Thompson’s criticism of Hardy is reported through Carter, not freshly checked against either original. Carter expressly retains the inescapable property dimension while considering a negotiated public divorce mechanism. No independent validation of every example or generalized personal formation is claimed.

proposals.relationship: Carter uses Wolfe’s logic-of-elimination framework when interpreting the dispossession and exclusion underlying prairie homesteading.
proposals.evidence_note: Imperial Plots 6/note6 explicitly names Wolfe and applies the formulation within her analysis of land, reserves and excluded Indigenous farmers. The note cites his 2006 Journal of Genocide Research article,387; the bibliography supplies387–409. The article remains unread in this dossier. This is a bounded resource in the 2016 book, read in its corrected 2018 reprint, not an influence inferred from citation alone or a retrospective classification of all Carter’s earlier work. Earlier edge_1315 retains its limits.

proposals.relationship: Carter uses Philippa Levine’s gender-and-empire analysis to explain why profitable colonial masculinity excluded women and colonized people.
proposals.evidence_note: Imperial Plots 7–8/notes13,20 explicitly frames the male imperial settler and quotes Levine’s particular exclusion argument. The bibliography identifies her authored Introduction: Why Gender and Empire? in her edited Gender and Empire (Oxford,2004); notes cite6–7. Authorship of this introduction is distinct from editing the collection and from Catherine Hall’s separate chapter. The original is unread here; this is a specific conceptual resource, not exclusive formation or a claim about Lawrence Levine.

proposals.relationship: Carter uses Tosh alongside Levine to frame the gendered ideal of the white male settler as an imperial producer.
proposals.evidence_note: Imperial Plots 7/note13 jointly cites Levine’s introduction,6, and Tosh’s Manliness and Masculinities in Nineteenth-Century Britain (2005),183–185, for this framing. This is a shared bibliographic and conceptual resource in her argument, not attribution of the quoted wording specifically to Tosh, sole intellectual origin, formal mentorship, or fresh reading of his book. The bibliography supplies the subtitle Essays on Gender, Family and Empire and Pearson/Longman publication.
